author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

text:
LLM has no common sense when writing RTL

Instead of giving me simple combination logic, it precomputed all the possible inputs into a giant table, then write a one line table look up.

The scary part, 9 out 10 times, LLM gives me a good combination logic, the 10th time it suddenly goes stupid, give me a giant look up table

author.name: Michał Piszczek
author.headline: CTO @ Archdesk | FinTech exit | Ex-hacker | Building AI systems that actually work | AI infrastructure · Security Mechanics · Frontier Shifts · SaaS execution | Physics × Economics × Execution

comments.text: The 9 out of 10 is what makes it dangerous, not the 10th. A reviewer who has seen nine clean outputs stops reading the tenth as carefully, and a lookup table synthesizes fine in simulation right up until it blows your gate count and timing closure on the actual chip.

author.headline: Senior Data Engineer | 12+ YoE | AWS • GCP • PySpark • Kafka • RAG | 🌍 Open to Global Roles

replies.text: Michał Piszczek just need LLM which check previous LLM answers, etc, etc  😋

comments.text: This is why we developed Python to Verilog as an intermediate logical level. The LLM writes in high level and our compiler generates optimized Verilog code according to PPA tradeoff directives.
